results.summary: This chip implements two games: tic-tac-toe (two-player) and rock-paper-scissors (player vs. machine). Game selection and moves are input via the ui pins, and outputs indicate game state, winner, or draw. The rock-paper-scissors opponent uses a 3-bit LFSR to generate pseudo-random choices. External hardware such as an LED display can be connected for easier viewing of the outputs.

Choreo8 is an 8-LED pattern generator that produces effects such as Knight Rider, waves, and sparkles. It uses a 5 MHz clock and an internal divider to offer fast (4 Hz) and slow (1 Hz) update modes, selected by an input pin. The pattern is chosen via three select pins, and an enable and pause input control operation. The design drives eight output pins directly connected to LEDs.

This project implements a 2-layer binary neural network (BNN) that classifies an 8-bit input into one of four categories (turn left, turn right, stop, U-turn). It uses XNOR-popcount operations instead of multipliers, and supports real-time weight loading via a 4-bit bidirectional interface. The design is intended for educational and demonstrational purposes, showing simple ML on-chip without CPUs or RAM. Testing is done with CocoTB, and accuracy is limited due to the small network size.

This design is an 8x8-to-16-bit multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit with a 2-cycle 8-bit serial interface for data input and output. It supports both signed and unsigned arithmetic and includes overflow detection and clear functionality. The MAC is intended for DSP applications and fits within the TinyTapeout I/O constraints by using a serial protocol. No external hardware is required beyond the standard clock and reset.

This is a 4-bit digital-to-analog converter (DAC) that converts a 4-bit digital input into an analog output current or voltage. It is implemented in analog circuitry and has one analog output pin. Testing can be done using a pseudo-random binary sequence (PRBS) to evaluate dynamic range and output current. The documentation is minimal, providing only basic functionality and a suggestion for testing.

This analog design compares a threshold voltage and generates a current output. It has six analog pins including LED, voltage sense, and control signals, and many digital pins tied to ground. The documentation is very sparse, stating only that it compares threshold voltage and generates current, and that testing requires a function generator and oscilloscope. The design appears to be a mixed-signal circuit with an LED driver and voltage sensing, but details are lacking.

This chip implements a reaction time test where a user presses a start button, waits for an LED to light up after a random delay, and then presses a react button as quickly as possible. The reaction time is displayed in milliseconds on a 4-digit 7-segment display, and cumulative times are shown until reset. If the react button is pressed before the LED, an error message is displayed. Silicon testing revealed that the design is broken: the start button does not start the test, reset does not work, and pressing react puts it in an error state, though it worked on an FPGA.

This project is a compact 4-channel fractional-N phase-locked loop (PLL) frequency synthesizer intended for next-generation systems-on-chip. It is controlled via a simple CSR interface using input pins for data and address, and outputs four independent clock channels plus an ADC output for control voltage monitoring. The design is implemented in Verilog and targets a 10 MHz reference clock. The documentation is extremely minimal, providing only pin descriptions and no detailed explanation of operation or testing.

This is a 4-point, 8-bit fixed-point Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) engine implemented in SystemVerilog. It uses a radix-2 decimation-in-time architecture with butterfly modules and twiddle factor multiplication to compute the frequency-domain representation of four complex samples. The design interfaces with switches for control, a bidirectional data bus for samples and results, and a single-digit 7-segment display for status. External hardware includes a 7-segment display, switches, and a reset button.

This project implements a modified Izhikevich neuron model in 22-bit fixed-point arithmetic to capture various spiking behaviors. It uses select pins to choose neuron parameters and five input pins for current injection, with outputs for membrane potential and recovery variable. The design is intended for simulating spiking cortical neurons in digital hardware, and external observation requires inverting the outputs and connecting to an oscilloscope. The documentation includes equations and a testbench description, but no silicon test results are provided.
